source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Models can judge their own sampled answers (P(True)). Larger models do this better. Few-shot calibration is good; zero-shot is worse.
numbers: Anthropic models up to 52B; tasks TriviaQA, GSM8k, arithmetic, Lambada, Codex. Answers with P(True)>0.5 are far more often correct than generic samples.
limits: Self-evaluation of own samples; zero-shot calibration is poor. Closest analogue of a retrospective confidence judgment, not a before-answer feeling of knowing.
agent_relevance: Cheap post-hoc check for states that verify an answer; works better with several samples shown.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Showing the model many of its own T=1 samples before it rates one sample improves self-evaluation. This resembles self-consistency as a confidence cue (Koriat-style).
numbers: Brier score best for comparison-sample prompts (fixed or 20-shot) in every task in the appendix comparison; k-shot helps mostly by fixing calibration, not discrimination.
limits: Needs multiple samples (cost). Brier does not fall with size on Codex because small-model samples are nearly all invalid.
agent_relevance: Sample-then-judge is a usable confidence signal for the agent loop.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: P(IK): a value head trained on bare questions predicts whether the model will answer correctly BEFORE answering. This is the machine version of feeling of knowing / ease-of-learning.
numbers: Trained on TriviaQA, 52B P(IK) separates known from unknown questions in-distribution; AUROC rises with model size. Trained on TriviaQA alone, it transfers to math, Lambada and code with decent AUROC; training on all tasks improves every task (Table 1).
quote: we only find partial generalization on this task
limits: Only partial generalization. On Lambada calibration was terrible because P(IK) was uniformly low until trained on all four tasks. Needs training; a prompt-only version is weaker.
agent_relevance: Supports an S0 gate that predicts task difficulty from the question alone, but a trained probe is needed for good calibration on new task classes.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: P(IK) responds in the right direction to context: higher with relevant source text and correct hints, lower with distracting hints. Models predict their own P(IK) slightly better than another model's.
numbers: Own-vs-other: models somewhat better at predicting their own P(IK); crossing training data gives a small effect. Tested on GSM8k hints and source materials.
limits: Small effect for own-versus-other; two models of about equal capability only.
agent_relevance: Gate should be re-run after retrieval or hints are added, since the feeling of knowing changes with context, as in humans.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: RLHF policies are miscalibrated on token probabilities, but a temperature change largely repairs this.
numbers: RLHF 52B policies on MMLU, MMLU True/False, TruthfulQA; calibration curves at T=1 vs T=2.5 (Fig. 9).
limits: Section 3.3 only; later work (Tian 2023) finds RLHF models need verbalized rather than token confidence.
agent_relevance: Do not trust raw token confidence from chat models; recalibrate.

source: Lin, Hilton, Evans (2022) Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words
finding: A GPT-3 model finetuned to say a confidence in words ('90%') is calibrated, and stays moderately calibrated under distribution shift. First such result.
numbers: CalibratedMath suite; trained on Add-subtract only, tested on Multiply-divide and Multi-answer. Verbalized probability generalizes reasonably to both (text of Sec 3.2; table cell values were garbled in extraction, so not quoted).
limits: Finetuning needed (100 questions per sub-task plus zero-shot answers). Arithmetic only. Model is claimed to use latent uncertainty, not just copy logits.
agent_relevance: Verbal confidence is learnable, but a scaffold without finetuning has to rely on prompts (see Tian 2023).

source: Yin et al. (2023) Do Large Language Models Know What They Don't Know?
finding: SelfAware benchmark tests whether a model can tell unanswerable from answerable questions. GPT-4 is best but below humans.
numbers: 1,032 unanswerable + 2,337 answerable questions; 20 LLMs. GPT-4 F1 75.47% vs human 84.93%.
limits: Unanswerable is not the same as 'I do not know this fact'; the measure is a classification task, not item-level feeling of knowing.
agent_relevance: Calibrates expectation: even the best model misses about a quarter, so the gate must be soft.

source: Yin et al. (2023) Do Large Language Models Know What They Don't Know?
finding: In-context examples and instruction tuning raise self-knowledge. Bigger models do better.
numbers: Davinci: in-context examples give +27.96% over direct input. Vicuna-13B beat LLaMA-65B, credited to instruction tuning.
limits: Prompt design effect confounded with model family.
agent_relevance: A few worked examples in the gate prompt can lift 'know vs unknown' detection a lot.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? Black-box confidence elicitation
finding: Verbalized confidence from LLMs is overconfident and a poor failure predictor. GPT-4 is better but still weak.
numbers: 5 LLMs, 8 tasks. GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7% (near 50% chance). GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna average ECE above 0.377. AUROC about 22.2% better from GPT-3 to GPT-4. White-box vs black-box gap in AUROC 0.522 to 0.605.
limits: Professional-knowledge tasks hard for every method; no method wins everywhere.
agent_relevance: Do not build the gate on one verbalized number from the model.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? Black-box confidence elicitation
finding: Consistency over several samples beats a single verbalized confidence at predicting failure, most on arithmetic.
numbers: GSM8K AUROC 54.8% (single verbalized) to 92.7% (5 samples with consistency aggregation). Human-inspired prompts reduced ECE but left AUROC near chance. GPT-4 with 93.6% GSM8K accuracy got ECE 0.064 by saying 100% for everything, a trivial calibration.
limits: Cost of k samples. ECE alone can be gamed; AUROC shows the problem.
agent_relevance: Use sample agreement as the main signal, with ECE and AUROC both reported.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: For RLHF models (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude 2) verbalized confidence is better calibrated than token probabilities. Asking for several candidate answers first helps more ('consider the opposite').
numbers: TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA; verbalized prompts cut ECE by a relative 50% in many cases (abstract: 'often reducing').
limits: Calibration gain, not discrimination; the later Xiong study shows AUROC stays weak.
agent_relevance: Prompt-only route to a usable confidence; add a 'list alternatives first' step.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What large language models know and what people think they know
finding: People over-trust default LLM explanations, and longer explanations raise confidence without raising accuracy. Matching the explanation's tone to the model's real confidence narrows the gaps.
numbers: 301 participants across two experiments (284 retained); multiple-choice and short-answer; calibration gap and discrimination gap both narrowed when explanations reflected model confidence.
limits: Online participants; confidence read from model internals.
agent_relevance: Output length is a false cue for confidence in humans (a fluency effect); the agent's reports should match its real confidence.

source: Steyvers & Peters (2025) Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Humans and LLMs
finding: Review comparing human and LLM metacognition. Humans and LLMs are both overconfident. LLM confidence from response consistency parallels Koriat's self-consistency model of human confidence.
numbers: Example AUC for correct-vs-incorrect confidence: 0.778 (GPT-3.5, token likelihoods on MMLU) and 0.83 (finetuned GPT-4.1-mini, TriviaQA). Cites Cash et al. (2025) finding similar human and LLM sensitivity.
quote: consistency across internally simulated alternatives may serve as a basis for confidence
limits: Cash et al. used AUROC2, which is confounded with accuracy, and did not control accuracy (the review's own caveat). Review, not new data.
agent_relevance: Strongest bridge from Koriat's cue theory to LLM practice: agreement among internal candidates is the cue.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know
finding: Prompting alone is not enough; finetuning on a small graded set gives a good uncertainty estimator. Sampling gives calibration but weak discrimination; verbal elicitation gives decent discrimination but poor calibration.
numbers: About 1,000 graded examples suffice to beat baselines (LoRA, ~20,000-example pool). Probe on frozen features beats baselines on multiple-choice MMLU; open-ended needs training through the model.
limits: Open models only. A user study shows uncertainty estimates change how people use LLMs.
agent_relevance: If we can grade 1,000 past runs, a small learned difficulty predictor beats any prompt-based gate.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know
finding: A model can estimate other models' uncertainty too, so a separate small judge is possible.
numbers: Abstract: many models work as general-purpose uncertainty estimators, applicable to their own and other models' uncertainty.
limits: Details of cross-model gaps not extracted.
agent_relevance: A cheap separate model could run the S0 gate.

source: Binder et al. (2024) Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection
finding: After finetuning on its own behaviour, a model predicts its own behaviour in hypothetical situations better than another model trained on the same data. Privileged access.
numbers: Llama-3-70B beats GPT-4o at predicting Llama-3-70B by +17% accuracy; self-prediction is better calibrated; holds after behaviour is changed by finetuning.
limits: Works only on simple tasks; fails on complex tasks and out-of-distribution generalization; no chain-of-thought allowed in self-prediction.
agent_relevance: Self-prediction of difficulty may work for simple classes but should not be trusted on novel ones.

source: Cheng et al. (2024) Can AI Assistants Know What They Don't Know?
finding: Aligning a model with a model-specific Idk dataset (its own known and unknown questions) lets it refuse most unknown questions, and accuracy on answered ones rises.
numbers: Idk dataset from TriviaQA: 45.05% known-answerable, 54.95% unknown. Idk-Prompting truthful rate 66.93%; Idk-SFT 74.75% but with an 'alignment tax' (fewer known questions answered); DPO, best-of-N, PPO, HIR also tested.
limits: Model-specific labels needed; refusal can cost correct answers.
agent_relevance: Direct test of 'knowing that you do not know' with a measurable cost: abstain too often and you lose answers.

source: Gekhman et al. (2024) Does Fine-Tuning LLMs on New Knowledge Encourage Hallucinations?
finding: An LLM learns facts it does not already know much more slowly than facts it knows, and learning them raises hallucination linearly. A judgment-of-learning type result for machines: known vs unknown material differs in learnability.
numbers: Closed-book QA, fine-tuning mix of Known and Unknown examples; best dev accuracy when most Known but few Unknown examples are fitted.
limits: Fine-tuning setting, not in-context learning.
agent_relevance: Warns against forcing the agent to act on facts it cannot ground; unknown items are costly to absorb.

source: Ferrando et al. (2025) Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in LMs
finding: Sparse-autoencoder directions in Gemma 2 and Llama 3.1 tell the model whether it recognizes an entity. They are causal: steering makes the model refuse about known entities or hallucinate about unknown ones. This matches the familiarity cue view of feeling of knowing.
numbers: Steering with the unknown-entity latent gives almost 100% refusal across entity types in Gemma 2 2B. On songs released after the cutoff the unknown-entity latent fires 53% (Gemma 2 2B), 55% (Gemma 2 9B), 76% (Llama 3.1 8B) versus known-entity latent 6%, 22%, 13.4%.
limits: Entities only (athletes, songs, movies, cities); small open models.
agent_relevance: Recognition of the topic comes before recall, as in human cue-familiarity accounts; the gate can look at familiarity of the question's entities.

source: Orgad et al. (2025) LLMs Know More Than They Show
finding: Truthfulness information is concentrated in the exact answer tokens, probes there detect errors best, but probes do not transfer across datasets. A model can encode the right answer and still output a wrong one.
numbers: AUC peaks at exact answer tokens (Mistral-7b-instruct, layer-by-token map, Fig. 2).
limits: Probes are task-specific, so 'truthfulness' is not one universal direction.
agent_relevance: Hidden monitoring signals exist but are task-specific; train per task class.

source: Azaria & Mitchell (2023) The Internal State of an LLM Knows When It's Lying
finding: A classifier on hidden-layer activations (SAPLMA) labels sentences true or false better than output probabilities.
numbers: 71% to 83% average accuracy depending on the base model; BERT baseline near chance on some sets.
limits: True/false statements, not question-level difficulty.
agent_relevance: Another route for a learned gate if hidden states are available.

source: Mallen et al. (2023) When Not to Trust Language Models
finding: Subject-entity popularity (Wikipedia page views) predicts whether a model knows a fact; scaling helps popular facts but not the long tail. Popularity is a cue like human familiarity.
numbers: PopQA: 14k questions. GPT-3 davinci-003 was 35% accurate overall (15-shot). Correlation of accuracy with log popularity is stronger for larger LMs. Adaptive Retrieval (retrieve only below a popularity threshold) lifted davinci-003 to 46.5%, 5.3% above any non-adaptive method.
limits: Popularity needs an external count; threshold is tuned per relation type.
agent_relevance: Closest working machine analogue of a feeling-of-knowing gate that decides whether to look things up.

source: Jeong et al. (2024) Adaptive-RAG
finding: A small classifier predicts query complexity and routes to no retrieval, single-step, or multi-step retrieval. This is a trained ease-of-learning gate inside an LLM pipeline.
numbers: A router using true labels (oracle) scores higher than the learned router (e.g. 45.00 vs 37.17 F1 in one column), so routing errors cost accuracy.
limits: Table partly garbled in extraction; only the oracle gap in one cell is quoted.
agent_relevance: Template for S0: label past tasks by which strategy succeeded, train a router.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) R-Tuning: Instructing LLMs to Say I Don't Know
finding: Tuning on refusal-aware data (refuse where the model's knowledge is missing) improves accuracy on questions it answers and the refusal skill transfers to other domains.
numbers: Evaluated with Average Precision (AP) over willingly answered questions, LLaMA-13B among models tested; abstract states learned uncertainty gives better calibration than uncertainty-based testing.
limits: Requires finetuning; per-dataset numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Abstention is a trainable meta-skill, not just a prompt.

source: Yona et al. (2024) Can LLMs Faithfully Express Their Intrinsic Uncertainty in Words?
finding: Models answer decisively even when they are uncertain, and when asked to hedge the hedges do not match their real uncertainty. Faithfulness metric: gap between decisiveness and intrinsic confidence.
numbers: Aligned LLMs tested on knowledge QA tasks (e.g. Natural Questions); abstract states modern LLMs are poor at faithful uncertainty.
limits: Intrinsic confidence estimated by sampling.
agent_relevance: Stated confidence must be checked against a consistency measure.

source: Zhou, Jurafsky, Hashimoto (2023) Navigating the Grey Area
finding: Words like 'I'm sure' put in a prompt change model accuracy, and high-certainty wording lowers accuracy. Models mimic wording rather than reflect knowledge state.
numbers: 50 epistemic markers injected into QA prompts; accuracy varies by more than 80% across markers; high-certainty expressions give a 7% drop versus low-certainty ones; factive verbs hurt, evidentials help.
limits: Prompt wording study, not a metamemory paradigm.
agent_relevance: Do not put confidence-boosting language into the scaffold prompts.

source: Didolkar et al. (2024) Metacognitive Capabilities of LLMs: Mathematical Problem Solving
finding: GPT-4 labels math problems with skills; at test time the model names the needed skill and gets matching worked examples. A metacognitive 'what kind of problem is this' step used inside a solving loop.
numbers: 11.6% gain over chain-of-thought on MATH; 3.5% over Complex CoT; 7.52% over PAL baseline.
limits: Math only; gains depend on the skill list quality.
agent_relevance: Template for S0 problem-class labeling that feeds example retrieval.

source: Ji-An et al. (2025) Language Models are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations
finding: With neurofeedback-style in-context examples, models can report and control some activation directions, but only a low-dimensional subset.
numbers: Ability depends on number of in-context examples, interpretability of the direction, and variance it explains.
limits: Abstract-level reading; paradigm is neuroscience-inspired, not a classic metamemory task.
agent_relevance: Self-monitoring is limited to a small slice of internal state, so do not expect full introspection.
